name: Thinkster Math
line: Thinkster pairs AI-made worksheets with a live tutor. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Thinkster Math: AI-made worksheets with a live tutor. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Thinkster Math's unit is the worksheet: practice its AI creates, with a video, reviewed by a tutor who meets the learner in live sessions [1][2]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after, right or wrong, updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Thinkster starts with an assessment of about seven minutes that maps skills and gaps [1]. After that, its mastery map updates after every worksheet [1].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a film where there is one, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Thinkster the unit is the worksheet: targeted practice its AI creates, with a video tutorial, and a tutor's feedback afterward [1]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [9].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After each problem AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. At Thinkster, explanation comes from a tutor, who leaves feedback on worksheets, and from an AI coach that guides with Socratic prompts and does not give the answer [1][2]. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [8].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer given after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped and does not count as learned. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. Thinkster says its engine traces a gap back through the concepts underneath it [1]. Its mastery map marks each skill green, yellow or red, and we found no stated rule for green [1][2].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. At Thinkster, the tutor reviews the learner's week of work in each session [1]. We found no schedule for bringing back skills already mastered in the pages we read [1][2]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [7].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 8, Algebra 1 and Geometry, aligned to Common Core and state standards [1][2].
rows.start: A separate assessment of about seven minutes that maps skills and gaps [1].
rows.teaching: Live 45-minute one-to-one tutor sessions, one to three a week, a video with each worksheet, and an AI coach at any hour [1][2].
rows.next: Its AI creates targeted practice and, it says, adjusts difficulty at each problem and traces gaps to earlier concepts [1].
rows.mastery: A mastery map, green for mastered, updated after every worksheet. We found no stated rule for green [1][2].
rows.review: The tutor reviews the week's work in each session [1]. We found no schedule for revisiting mastered skills [1][2].
rows.print: Printable worksheets by grade and topic, for practice at home [3].
rows.adult: A dedicated tutor reviews the learner's work and leads each session [1][2]. The adult follows a parent dashboard [2].
rows.reports: A parent dashboard and daily progress reports: problems worked, tutor feedback, skill mastery levels [1].
rows.evidence: No outcome study found, and no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse [4][5].

theirs: Thinkster Math is an online math tutoring service. Its maker describes it as tutoring personalized by patented AI and top math tutors [1]. A learner works with one dedicated tutor in live 45-minute one-to-one sessions, one to three times a week, and has an AI coach at any hour [1][2].

A learner starts with an assessment of about seven minutes that maps skills and gaps [1]. Day to day, the learner spends 15 to 20 minutes, five days a week, on worksheets of targeted practice that Thinkster's AI creates, each with a video tutorial [1]. The mastery map updates after every worksheet, tutors leave feedback on worksheets, and in each session the tutor reviews the learner's week of work [1]. The AI coach guides with Socratic prompts and does not give the answer [1][2].
credit: The same dedicated tutor in live one-to-one sessions, one to three times a week [2].
An engine built to tell a slip in calculation from a wrong idea [1].
An AI coach that guides with questions and does not give the answer [1][2].

theirs: We found no published study comparing Thinkster students' math learning with similar students who did not use it, and no Thinkster entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [4][5]. Its home page gives figures such as 3x faster learning, without naming a study behind them [1].

Tutoring in general has strong evidence. Across 263 randomized trials it averaged 0.40 standard deviations, and 0.16 to 0.22 in large U.S. programs measured on standardized tests [6]. That evidence is about tutoring, not about Thinkster.
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison: worked examples improve math performance across 55 studies [9], and practice that mixes and spaces topics scored 62% against 38% for practice in blocks a month later, in a randomized trial that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations [7]. AMP shows worked steps after every answer and brings learned skills back in ordinary practice, mixed with other math.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and the code is public.

them: You want your child to work with the same live tutor every week.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate test.
You want a hint, a lesson and the worked answer at every problem.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your child is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want to see the actual problems behind every number.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Thinkster Math?
questions.answer: Thinkster pairs worksheets its AI creates with a live tutor who reviews the learner's work [1][2]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Thinkster Math work?
questions.answer: We found no study comparing Thinkster students with similar students, and no entry in Evidence for ESSA or the What Works Clearinghouse [4][5]. Tutoring in general has strong evidence in randomized trials [6].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. AMP places a learner from their first answers, whatever else they use.
